blocks.x: Well you mentioned Pierron's band and what type of music they play. I forgot to mention it was in the year about 1915. I think Pierron then used mostly string instruments. And he played regular conventional ragtime like I had right on records that was of that date of error. There's some things I'd like to tell you that I may have forgotten to mention. We played for two silent movies. One of them is in the Good For Nothing by Carlisle Blackwell. He was the leading man. And her shot was Charlie Chapman. This would be the same shot as these pitchers were taken at Rice Weber's Restaurant in the 400 Club in 1970. And many other fairs for the Goulds. That's the Jay Gould family. Balls, political parties, theaters and concerts. Entertained over a million soldiers and Marines during the World War I. Sold Liberty bonds. Ballyhoed in the streets of New York City. Also at several stores in New York City. Had passes to all the forts for entertainments of the soldiers. And also entertain soldiers in different hospitals. Now, we get back to Pierron. Pierron is the man who instrumentally was mostly responsible for having this Clarence Williams come to New York. Clarence Williams came to the hotel where I live with a letter of introduction by Mr. Pierron, who I had corresponded with. Because I had already made Brown Skin famous and was published by Will Rossinger. You'll find cards to that effect in the Tulane repository. We'll prove to you that we didn't discriminate against the colored man. As been said by Marshall Steins and many others. In fact, we helped our colored brethren. You'll see here on one of these first tunes of Clarence Williams. They have My Pillar and Me by Tim Brown, Chris Smith and Clarence Williams. Clarence Williams Publishing Company, 1547 Broadway, New York City. On that, he's got a jazz tune. Now, he had never used this word before. I'm that positive that I don't have many years of my life to go. This was in 1923 that he came to New York. Before that, he was in Chicago. He was a talent scout for the Columbia where he and his wife, Eva Taylor, made recordings for Columbia. Now, if this music as they say existed and this Negro was one of the principal men of composing music, it certainly would have showed before 23, 24 and 25 that these other Negroes came up. And when they did come up, they were imitating the original Dixon and Jazz Band. Because I can show you the idioms eight years before these Negroes ever put it down on racks that they were used by the original Dixon and Jazz Band. Now, would you care to read this letter of P. Ron's? This is August 13, 1922.

This is a letter. It says, It says, From A.J. P. Ron, 1734 Annette Street, New Orleans, Louisiana. The dateline is August 13, 1922. Mr. D. James LaRocca, original Dixon and Jazz Band. 421 Sheets Head Bay Road, Brooklyn, New York. My dear Mr. LaRocca, yours of the fifth INST comp was received and very sorry indeed for the delay and great suspense that you no doubt suffered. But only to the fact that I was out of the city, I was unable to answer at once. But I assure you that I have taken great interest in saying, and in the future you can rest assured that all correspondents will receive my prompt attention. I'm not aware of the fact that you all are the starters of Sister Kate up north. That's quote Sister Kate, unquote, up north. But I wish to express my delight in being informed of saying through your letter of the fifth. And assure you that you will receive all assistance that I can give along the lines of placing this and all of the numbers that I have and that you may be able to use. I'm sorry indeed that you were put to such inconvenience in trying to locate me. And again, I am glad that you succeeded. As far as bands are concerned, you can rest assured that I will put forth every effort to keep them supplied with my numbers. And I really haven't the language to express my thanks for the splendid efforts made by both you and your band. Speaking of the victor concern, I feel sure that you will... Better read this slowly. Speaking of the victor concern, I feel sure that you will... I feel assured that you will meet with tremendous success due to the wide reputation of your aggregation. And while I am at it, and aside from Sister Kate, I am sending you to look over. If your man is like my man, that's a quote, if your man is like my man, unquote. And several others that have recently came into the limelight here. And I believe that from your letter of the fifth, we'll go over also for reasons aforementioned. In reference to paragraph five of your letter, we'll say that I am unable to make a complete statement concerning... Turning it over to a large pub concern, that's capital P-U-B concern. I presume that means publishing. Publishing concern. As I have already several contracts from different concerns to be considered. But in the meantime, I will appreciate anything you might do to record Sister Kate or any other number of mine. You can rest assured that you will be greatly recompensated for saying. Now in the event that any concern approach you with their willingness to accept, that's E-X-E-E-P-T, quote, Sister Kate, unquote, or any other number, you will do well to wire or write me at once so you will give me a chance to demonstrate to you my thanks. For some time I have felt that the title, quote, I wish that I could shimmy like my Sister Kate, unquote, was a little out of date. And for that reason I have changed it to, quote, Sister Kate, unquote, with a rearrangement of lyrics, and on a few days you will receive the new outfit, which I hope you can use to great advantage. Now trusting that you will be able to use the numbers that I am sending under separate cover, I am very, yours very truly, AJP Rome, and that has initials J-C-R-A-J-P.

Well this will show that I did try to help the colored man out, and I had no malice or thought of doing anybody anything that was out of the way of being honest with anyone. We featured these numbers that rise to others. We featured Brown Skin, Who You Follow, which Will Rossiter published. That's one of his numbers. We featured Mama's Baby Boy. Now, it's been said that we played many Negro melodies. That is true. Because we played many other tunes. Let me get back. And we also featured Sister Kate. It was all of the three of them. We had special arrangements on them. We used to get up. We didn't sing, but we used to holler, sing like we were trying to sing. In other words, it pleased the public. They liked what we were doing. And they'd ask for the same things over, and we'd play it.
Who did the singing of the band?

Five of us. You know what I mean? Yeah. I'd get up there and start, I wish I could Jimmy like my sister Kate. Da-da-da-da, da-da-da-da, da-da-da. And so on. It says, Mama's Baby Boy. Da-da-da-da-da-da-da. There were good numbers. And we played them. The same as some of these days. Downtown Strutters Ball. Or many other tunes that was owned by colored people we played. From that, all the people write about us, they said they played colored melodies. Sure, we played colored melodies. We also played melodies that were written by white people. But we didn't sing to white people's melodies. You don't ask me why? I don't know. Because they were made different. In other words, when we got out there, who you for? Brown skin, I'm for you white folks. Stuff like that. That would appeal to the northern man. But I'd get out there somewhere, and I'd have to have a good voice to sing that. You understand? It was more of a more popular tune. And we weren't going out there and saying something that everybody sang. Because we'd be making fools out of ourselves. We'd sound like a bunch of bullfrogs. Singing against a man that could sing. And these other tunes, we didn't need much voice to sing them. And we made them popular. Now this was between the years of 1921, 1919. In 21 and 22, Sister Kate. We sang that at Top and Wagey Garden. That's when we made that popular. Around 21 or 1920. But the others were prior to that. Now he had sent me these tunes. From time to time, he'd send me numbers. I had never known of Clarence Williams in my life. But Clarence Williams in the orchestra world in 1936, he has an article in the orchestra world. It says, From Honky Tongue to Swing. An interview by Clarence Williams. Well, this is a kind of long article.

You want me to read the part of it? Now you were going to correct that date back there. You said 1819, and that just couldn't be right. 1918. That was 1918. And this was the years the tunes were popular that you were talking about. You were saying these colored melodies.
You were playing the brown scale, who you fought?
It started around 1819. And when did it last? 1918. You see, 1819. It started around.
I got a role too. We played them all the way through London. They weren't in all.
Yes.

We played the same pieces through London. Wherever we went, we played them. As dance tunes, you know? We used them as novelties. I see. Along with our other novelists, we had, you couldn't just give them dry music all the time. You got out there, you did a little humming and singing. I sang Margie before it was even published and made a hit out of it. I haven't got no voice. Is it recording now?
Yes, it's recording.

And this is what I'd like you to read. It was in 1918. If I got 1819 down there, it's the wrong date. I wasn't even in. It would have to be 1918 that we had these Mama's Baby Boy and Brown Skin, who you fought? I want you to read this here, part of an article. He says, Swing, as they call it today, by Clarence Waino. From Honky Tonk to Swing.

All right. Let's see. This is from Orchestra World, 1936. Let's see. All right. Swing, as they call it today, was originated in New Orleans, the birthplace of Sister Kate and many other standard swing tunes, such as Tiger Rag. In those days, you could find in the slums of New Orleans such places as the Red Onion, the Keystone, Pete Lawless, and the Odd Fellows Hall, where the Eagle Band used to play. The Eagle Band was one of the highest bands in the country, with Buddy Bolden Cornetis, who had the world beat when it came to swing and jazz. Clarence stated that he heard him play when he, Clarence, was six or eight years old, and he was playing this same tune now called Tiger Rag, to which his mother and father used to dance the quadrille. That's spelled, quote, C-O-R-D-R-E-E-L, unquote. What he meant is quadrille.
Yeah.

It is an original Negro tune, which was made up down south. It was named Tiger Rag when the Dixieland Band brought it up north. Buddy, you want me to continue with this? Yeah, go on. Buddy Bolden was the hottest cornetist in the world, and he played so much that he is in the insane asylum now if he is still living. After this time came King Oliver, Punk, and Freddie Capron, that's spelled K-E-P-P-E-R-T, and the original Creole Band. They were the last word and swing cornet players. The swing pianists were Albert K-A-L, Cal, I suppose that's Carroll, Lewis Wade, Clarence Williams, Tony Jackson, Steve Lewis, and Jelly Roll Morton. The seventh book된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된

We used to have swing sessions every morning around 3 o'clock after the boys got through with their work and each man would do his bit. Quote, the first hot band to leave from the South and introduce swing music was the Creole Jazz Band, unquote, says Mr. Williams. Quote, following the Dixieland Jazz Band, which recorded Livery Stable Blues and Tiger Ray, which swept the country. The Creole Band was colored and the Dixieland Band was white and they used to play across the street from each other and used to sit in for each other during rest periods. Then came King Oliver's Band to Chicago and Jimmy Noon's combination, that's spelled J-I-M-M-Y, Noon, and Eddie South, who was just a kid at the time. Then Chicago became the music center as all of the boys were leaving New Orleans. This was about 1917 when Chicago was full of swing bands at the Deluxe, the Dreamland, and the Royal GAR Hyphen. Is that the finish of it? Let's see, now that's... Oh, I'm sorry, it continues on. Here's a continuation. The Royal Garden, the Sunset, and others. They used to have swing sessions right on the street when they were advertising dances. Each band would be in a wagon covered with signs and would ballyhoo and try to sway the mind of the public to come to their affair. There were sometimes as many as four competitive bands on the same corner, and the best band would get the biggest crowd. King Oliver is the man who invented the wah-wah with the trumpet, the style that Clyde McCoy is using today.
I thought it was Celestine invented that. That's what they said, Celestine invented that. Clyde McCoy used it. Now King Oliver invented it.

Go ahead. The man who took it from King Oliver and added the plunger was Johnny Dunn, who was with Mamie Smith's Jazz Hounds and Lou Leslie's Plantation Review. It's a continuation all of the same quote. The first recording bands were the Dixieland Jazz Band. Go ahead. W.C. Smith... He played no jazz. I wonder who W.C. Smith is. Could that be Joseph Smith?
Joseph Smith.

Well, Paul Whiteman, Kid Tua Jazz. Mamie Smith and her jazz hands. I have them records of all of them. Clarence Williams' Blue Five and the Clarence Williams' Blue Rhythm Band, which was featuring Louis Armstrong, Donald Redmond, that's spelled R-E-D-M-O-N-D, Busta Bailey, Coleman Hawkins, etc. Louis Armstrong's first record that brought him recognition was Everybody Loves My Baby, which he recorded with the Clarence Williams' Blue Five. Fletcher Henderson and Benny Morton of Kansas City were also...
They were imitators of the Dixieland Jazz Band. Fletcher Henderson was one of the first colored men to copy from the records of the Dixieland Jazz Band.
Fletcher Henderson and Benny Morton of Kansas City were also among the first swing artists. Benny Morton's name is spelled M-O-R-T-O-N. Do you want me to read the letter to the editor? Just a moment.

These Negroes showed their appreciation after I had made it easy for them to come up and open his publishing concern. He didn't know me. That 20 years had passed. In 1936, Lou Gensler had a big broadcast. He tried to locate us to put us in the beginning and Benny Goodman as the end. In other words, the beginning and end. At this time, all these prophets got up in arms against us. John Hammond was one of them. He worked for Handy, I suppose, some kind of cheap lawyer or something on that order. And Handy was given out about jazz. He had given the definition of jazz to Abby Miles, what jazz music was about. He couldn't play it. They were up in arms that we were coming back to reclaim our position in the music world. This fellow, Marshall Stein, made a story about me. And he used Lloyd Kenner and Tom Brown as arch conspirators to say things that were untrue. Later on, Stein admitted to me in a letter that he only exaggerated because they didn't give the Negroes a break in this business. Can you stop the machine so I'm fine?
All right, go ahead.

When I brought the band up to New York, I went to a lawyer. The lawyer told me to go over there and talk to him. And asked this Mr. Williams, did he stand behind what he mentioned in the paper. In this article, Honky Tonk to Swing. I explained to him who I was before I showed him any correspondence of the paper on or anything else. I said, do you stand behind what you say? I said, I'm going to take you to court to make you prove. There's this correction right there. Like all Negroes, when you put them on the top of a horse, they ride them to death. This Negro never would have been to New York had it been for the original Dixieland jazz band. He and all the rest of the Negroes that come from New York and New Orleans. They never would have made good unless they styled themselves on the original Dixieland recordings.
You want me to read this now?
I want you to read that there.

This is from Orchestra World. Well, November 1936, letters to the editor. For the record, gentlemen, there is a correction I would like to make in the interview with me appearing in the October issue. In the third paragraph of the article, From Honky Tonk to Swing, I stated that I heard the same tune now called Tiger Rag when I was six or eight years old. Instead of the word same, I meant to say that the tune was somewhat similar to Tiger Rag. Mr. Williams has quoted same, and has put the word same in quotes, and has put the word similar in quotes. So it reads, instead of the word same, I mean to say the tune was somewhat similar to Tiger Rag. I would appreciate this correction very much, but it is not my intention to discredit Mr. Perrin Nick, Perrin Baraka as a composer of Tiger Rag, Clarence Williams Music Publishing Company, Inc. Perrin Baraka.

Now, I just showed you the kind of propaganda that the people put out. They all knew about Tiger Rag. Now, here's a Negro. I'm going to give you his record. And if I'm wrong, then the world is wrong. This Negro lived in Plaquemine, Louisiana, at the age of about six to eight years old, worked as a shoeshine boy for Ferdinand Herbert, who operated a barbershop in Plaquemine, Louisiana. He came to New Orleans in his late teens. He lies as to hearing Buddy Bowling play. From the dates given in the second line of pro-Negro propaganda, Bowling was incarcerated in the crazy house in 1906. He or Bowling would never remember them. And I'm almost going on to 70 years old. And I never heard Bowling play. And Bowling was supposed to live on the eight blocks from me, back Jackson Avenue. And I never heard him. And if he was popular in music, I certainly would have known something about him, because I play most every night in the week. Now, these neighbors here, they go on fiction. And stories that has been told for a generation down. There's the big man. Supposed to say the same thing about my father. Oh, he's Italian. He couldn't play that. They couldn't play nothing. There ain't nobody. My daddy played music too. And he played a horn. I didn't say that you could hear him down in Memphis, Tennessee. Like they said that they heard Bowling down in Memphis, Tennessee. Where Handy took down his notes when he played. All this is fabulous lies. Created by a bunch of pro-communists, pro-Negro intelligents who are trying to give the Negro culture. Now, they have did plenty damage. Yet, if I went to court, it would take me all the money I got to prove that they did damage, in a way, a monetary damage to me. In other words, it could tell my royalties anything. They have never did that. They have tried to discredit me in many things because when they look at Tiger Ride, that's the essence of American music as played today. And they ought to discredit that. You have men like Marshall Stein, John Hammond, Dr. Sushaw, who's supposed to know about this music. Let me read you Dr. Sushaw's letter, or have it read into this thing here, in 1949. Would you read this letter of Dr. Sushaw's in there?

No. It's going now. This is a letter. At the head is Dr. Admiral Sushaw, New Orleans. They, December 29, 1949. Dear Mr. LaRock, resuming our conversation of last night, I would simply write to repeat. The Marcus of Donegal wrote me and asked me to communicate to you. His address is, the Marcus of Donegal, 16 High Park Gate, London, SWF, England. As you know, Lord Donegal is head of all the jazz clubs of Great Britain. They're planning to have a 30-year centennial commemorating the opening up of the original Dixie Land Jazz Band in Hammersmith's Palais. On the exact same date you fellas opened up 30 years ago. It is going to be a national celebration of some sorts, and they would like to have you as a guest for the occasion. They would not ask you to play unless they wish you to play. I don't think they know that you are a very married man, but I will tell Lord Donegal of your fine wife and children, and I feel sure that he will include her in the invitation. Lord Donegal would like you to write him as soon as you can and answer all the above information. Also, would you give him the exact date that you opened up, so they can plan their celebration on that exact date. He also expresses his desire to borrow some old photographs of the old gang for them to use both for publicity, etc. The reason I am writing all these details is that I want you and Lord Donegal to deal with each other directly, and I don't want to become involved as a third party. However, if I can be of any assistance, don't hesitate to call on me. Please count on me as fully realizing the important position which you, which is underlying you, occupy as a member of the Pioneer Band and what you and your group has done for New Orleans. There is no confusion in my mind between white music and colored music, nor the relative merits of each. There never was and never will be any but one ODJB that started the whole thing. Sincerely, Edmond Sushan, M.D.

Well, that'll go to show you how a man can speak out of both sides of his mouth. I received a letter. Now, there's been plenty going on after Marshall Steins had given Tom Brown this favorable write-up. Brown was to go to different papers and have this printed and show it as real history. This was lying history connived by this man, Marshall Steins, who somewhere along in the front of these reels, you'll read his letter that he admitted to me he was lying. Now, they come up with more lies. There's a man from France, Mr. Avedy is his name. He wrote Howard Jacobs and asked him and sent an article in the paper that he would like to reach some old jazz man. I was one of the men that corresponded with him. I think Tom Brown may have had because he's got some of Tom Brown's stuff in there. And he may have contacted this fellow, Morez and Walter Cotfield. Would you read this letter here?
The entire letter you will.
Yeah, I think it should be. It may take a little longer.
Yeah, that's all right. Well, I guess we're about to take. It'll run out, but that's all right.

This letter he is about to read now. I've come across it by accident. It will show a man how he spoke out of both sides of his mouth. 1949, he said that there was no other band. Now he's promoting Tom Brown, who is recording and who is a member, and got 30 pieces of silver in the form of a loving cup, like Judas Iscariot got when he sold Christ. Would you please read that article from Mr. Sushant?
All right. This is the letter. The heading is... No dating on it. Dr. Edmond Sushant. No all names there.

Dear Stuart, thought you'd like a copy of these snaps. Do wish that I could get some together with you and Tom Brown some night soon. And deeply, as it says here, I am deeply regretful that you got away without playing a note last Saturday night, even though you gave me that, quote, I got a new horn and can't blow it yet, unquote. I was not going to let you get away without showing those guys, well, they call you Red Hot. That's underlined from I was not going down through Red Hot. Speak to Tom some night soon and ask him what would be convenient for them to get together some night next week, and I'll try to do my best to be right there. All right. Incidentally, we need a good picture of Tom in his prime as, quote, look, unquote, magazine, is here in town now and figures to run a story on New Orleans jazz. I told them what a great figure Tom was. Do you think he would spare me one for them? Best regards, Ed Marr.

Well, that'll show you what kind of people that the jazz club has and at the head of it. He wrote me in 1949 that I have proof that we were the original Dixieland jazz band. Now he's writing up on this guy that he is the original Dixieland jazz band. They give him a cup for his presence of being in the jazz club. What wonderful people they have in New Orleans. All they were doing was to start integration, what they call the mixing bowl. They had started that up north 22 years ago, 20 years ago, by Marshall Stein. Here's the first one started that business. It was brought to New Orleans. Yes. Yes. Many of my letters to different people. I've always mentioned the name is the history of jazz compiled by muggle heads, dope fiends, com-late prophets, self-aggrandizers, and many of these supposed to be historians filling their pocket up on poor, unfortunate musicians who never made anything at this music in the beginning. And now find a way that they can exploit these unfortunate men. And they're glad to get their name in the paper. So I listened to this propaganda. And I thought I was living in Russia, not the United States, the way some of this stuff was going on. My first idea was to try and interest someone into this kind of stuff was going on. I read in the paper where Senator Eastland was at the head of that committee. And he was from Mississippi. I wrote Senator Eastland, although he has never replied to me, but some action has been done in this matter. Do you want me to read it or you read this? I'll read it. All right. This is 1955.

This is a letter headed Dominique James Nicola Rocca, 2218 Constant Street, New Orleans, Louisiana, 13, January the 9th, 1955. Senator Eastland of Mississippi, Washington, D.C. Honorable Senator Eastland, Hoping you may direct your committee attention to the propaganda that has been going on in New Orleans. Because wherever there is smoke, there must be fire. These people have given out history, read jazz music, as compiled by the Northern Coppetbaggers, NAACP through Bill Handy, trying to give the Negro culture into the music field. This thing was started by one Marshall Stearns, a young Jewish scholar not out of school, who wrote lies about me and my band, the original Dixieland jazz band, the first jazz band in the world, migrated to Chicago, 1916, New York City, Rosenweber's Cafe, 1917, recorded for the Victor Company, record released March 7, 1916. 17? I'm sorry. You caught me there. Let me erase that. I made a mistake that was March the 7th, 1917, sold all over the globe, and perpetuated long before these men who write on jazz was born. I thought it was in Russia only where this kind of propaganda could be used by station WDSU, New Orleans item WDSU radio. Your Honor, I always thought the airways were for the public, radio, television, for newspapers, or a public service, found by moral decency to tell the truth. These carpetbaggers are aided in New Orleans by Ms. Myra Menville and Dr. Sushan, who are having mixed bands brought to New Orleans and given concerts, which is a method that was started by the historians having colored and white mixed to play. These people are from the intelligentsia and should know the laws of the South. These people control the press because of their position in the social world. They are supposed to be historians and pass on to who started this music. This jazz club movement is nothing but to bring on integration between the poor white man and the colored race, as these parasites are already segregated from their own poor, their own, I'm sorry, segregated from their own white poor people. They have their social circles where no poor white trash, as they have the Negro call us poor people. Please do not think I am a crank, but this bears looking into you. Sincerely, yours.
I want you to read this here about a nine-man court.

This is a nine-man court to hear appeal of Live Right from the New Orleans States Washington Bureau. They go on Washington. The appeal of Herman Live Right, former New Orleans television station director, from a contempt of Congress conviction, will be heard by the full nine-man United States Court of Appeals here, April 19... I'm sorry, April 23rd. The Live Right case, one of nine in a mass, but not consolidated hearing, will be taken up by the court at 10 a.m. Live Right and Allen bond were sentenced to three months in a prison in order to pay a $500 bond by U.S. Judge Richmond B. Keats more than a year ago after a jury had found him guilty on all 14 counts of an indictment charging contempt of Congress. The former WDSU television program director, 46, was accused of willfully refusing to answer questions asked him by the Senate Internal Security Subcommittee during an investigation of communism in the New Orleans. Other appeals will be heard from playwright Arthur Miller, newspaper man Robert Smelton, and William A. Price, John T. Gojack, Fort Wayne, Indiana labor leader, Norton Anthony Russell, engineer from Yellow Springs, Ohio, Bernard Deutsch, former student at the University of Pennsylvania, and Goldie Watson, Washington Dress Shoppe, owner. That's the end of the article. Another letter? Yeah. I think it's going on. Now this is a letter. D. James, Nick LaRocca, 2218 Constance Street, New Orleans, Louisiana, 13 February the 10th, 1957. Senator J.O. Eastland of Mississippi, Washington, D.C. Honorable Senator Eastland, the purpose of this letter is first to thank you for the conviction of Herman Leveride and to ask you to introduce a bill in Congress for a law to make it compulsory for television and radio stations to furnish a script. See, that was to make it compulsory for television and radio stations to furnish a script as to the programs they put on the air. This station, WDSU, has put on a program of lies against me and the ODJB. The two letters attached to this will tell my story. How can I sue them? They refused to furnish me with script of the program. I'm a poor man. I could not have the programs monitored. I'm sorry, that says, I could not have all their programs monitored.
